newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Jet fuel in Aug record high for month on jitters.
newsitem.headline: Jet fuel in Aug record high for month on jitters.

text.p: Asian jet fuel prices hit a record high in August compared with the same month in previous years as traders and refiners stock up in case prices jump sharply with escalating winter demand, traders said on Tuesday.
Physical prices have jumped to $28.70 per barrel, about $8.00 over the same period during the last two years, making some traders believe jet fuel has been overpriced, traders said.
On the paper market, bids for the jet fuel/gas oil spread have widened to $3.00 a barrel for September, $3.50 for October and up to $3.90 for November.

The price hike was due to airlines and traders hedging their positions on the paper market to avoid being caught by very high prices last season when severe northern hemisphere winter persisted until February, they said.
Prices reached a record high of nearly $34.00 at the peak of the winter season in January.
On the physical market some traders and refiners have stocked up kerosene in the Middle East, Guam and Singapore to prepare for the winter, traders said.

Prices have been on the uptrend since mid-June. It started with refiners maximising gas oil production in May, at the expense of jet fuel, because of healthy gas oil demand with India buying huge volumes during the first six months.

Shell Singapore's shutdown of its 200,000-barrel-per-day crude distillation unit for a month in early July worsened the shortage of jet fuel until refiners started to optimise jet fuel output instead.
Talk of Japanese refiners making enquiries for winter stockpiling also excited the market. But so far Japan has not started buying large volumes from the spot market for the winter, traders said.
However, Japan's imports in July, which rose nearly 110 percent over a year ago, indicated that their purchases this year would help to boost the market.

Japanese refiners' deliberate policy of limiting crude runs and keeping stocks low to help boost domestic prices would mean that imports could remain higher each month compared with last year, traders said.

On the other hand, some traders said the price rally might be due for a correction if the winter is not as severe as last year. That could prompt those holding jet fuel in storage to start dumping the cargoes on the market.

Traders also noted that unlike last year, when there were several refinery problems in Indonesia, Sri Lanka and India which caused serious disruptions and triggered higher demand, there has not been any sudden and serious refinery problems so far this year.

The only disruptions have been at two refineries in Australia as a result of a strike or technical glitches. The only effect following those problems at the Shell and Mobil refineries was the sale of two diesel and one kerosene cargo to Australia, which in turn cut back gasoline exports.
